lessons.title: Introduction to Booleans
lessons.summary: Until now, our Java programs have mostly followed instructions from top to bottom.

blocks.content: Until now, our Java programs have mostly followed instructions from top to bottom.
But real programs often need to make decisions based on whether something is true or false. For example:

- Giving a free delivery offer when an order reaches a certain amount.
- Showing "Pass" when a student's marks meet the required score.
- Allowing access only when the entered password is correct.
To build programs that can make these kinds of decisions, we first need to understand boolean values.

lessons.title: Booleans
lessons.summary:
- true
- false

blocks.text: A boolean is a Java data type used to represent one of two possible states:

blocks.content:
- true
- false
For example:

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.code:
true
false
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.content: Unlike int or double, a boolean cannot store numbers or decimal values. It can only represent true or false.
Boolean values are especially useful when a program needs to make decisions, such as checking whether a user is logged in, whether a payment was successful, or whether a student has passed.
In the next example, we'll see how Java determines these true and false values.

lessons.title: Understanding Boolean Values
lessons.summary: The values true and false are built-in boolean values in Java. They are different from strings and cannot be treated like ordinary variable names.

blocks.content: The values true and false are built-in boolean values in Java. They are different from strings and cannot be treated like ordinary variable names.

blocks.text: 1. Boolean Values Are Not Strings
When true is written without quotation marks, Java treats it as a boolean value.

blocks.code: boolean isAvailable = true;
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: However, "true" is text because it is enclosed in quotation marks:

blocks.code: String status = "true";
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: So, these two values have different data types:

- true → boolean
- "true" → String
Generally, true represents a positive condition, while false represents a negative condition.

blocks.text: 2. true and false Cannot Be Variable Names

blocks.content: true and false are reserved boolean literals in Java, so they cannot be used as variable names.
For example, this code is invalid:

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: Java will report an error because true already has a special meaning in the language.

However, names such as True or False are technically allowed because Java is case-sensitive. Still, using names that differ only by capitalization from boolean literals is not recommended because it can make your code confusing.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.content: true and false are boolean values, not strings and not variables.

lessons.title: Decision Making in Java
lessons.summary: Boolean expressions give us either true or false. Instead of only displaying these results, we can use them to control what the program does.

For example, a program can show a message only when a condition is satisfied.

Java provides the if statement to make such decisions.

blocks.content: In the next lesson, we'll learn how to use if statements in our programs.

lessons.title: The if Statement

lessons.title: The else if Clause
lessons.summary: An if...else statement lets us choose between two outcomes. When there are three or more possible outcomes, we can use else if.

blocks.content: An if...else statement lets us choose between two outcomes. When there are three or more possible outcomes, we can use else if.

blocks.text: Syntax

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: Java checks the conditions from top to bottom:

blocks.content:
- If the first condition is true, its block runs.
- If it is false, Java checks the else if condition.
- If all conditions are false, the else block runs.

blocks.text: Only one block is executed.

blocks.content: Let's understand this with an example next.

lessons.title: Introduction to Logical Operators
lessons.summary: For example:

blocks.text: Logical operators help us combine multiple conditions and make more useful decisions in Java.

blocks.content: For example:

- Check if a customer qualifies for a special offer when their order is above ₹2,000 and they are a member.
- Check if free delivery is available when the order is above ₹500 or the customer has a premium membership.
- Check whether a person meets the required conditions for an activity.
Next, we'll learn how logical operators combine conditions.

lessons.title: Logical Operators
lessons.summary: Next, we'll explore &&, ||, and ! with simple examples.

blocks.text: Java provides three logical operators that help us combine or modify conditions.

blocks.code:
Operator
Meaning
Example
&&

blocks.content: As programs become more complex, we often need to repeat the same task many times. For example, you may want to display a message 50 times.

Java provides loops to repeat instructions automatically, making our code shorter and easier to manage.
Let's learn how loops work and use them to build useful programs.

lessons.title: Introduction: break and continue
lessons.summary: Sometimes, a loop needs to behave differently instead of simply running from start to finish. For example:

blocks.content: Sometimes, a loop needs to behave differently instead of simply running from start to finish. For example:

- What if you need to end the loop immediately when a condition is met?
- What if you want to skip one iteration and continue with the next one?
Java provides two statements for controlling a loop's flow:

- break — stops the loop completely.
- continue — skips the current iteration and moves to the next one.

blocks.text: Let's first learn how the break statement works, then we'll explore continue.

lessons.title: Java break Statement
lessons.summary: As soon as Java reaches break, the loop ends immediately and execution continues with the code after the loop.

blocks.text: The break statement is useful when you want to stop a loop before it normally finishes.

blocks.content: As soon as Java reaches break, the loop ends immediately and execution continues with the code after the loop.

lessons.title: Java continue Statement
lessons.summary: The continue statement is used when you want to skip the remaining code for the current loop iteration.

blocks.content: The continue statement is used when you want to skip the remaining code for the current loop iteration.
Unlike break, continue does not stop the loop. After skipping the current iteration, the loop moves to the next one.
Here's how continue works in different loops:

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.summary: So far, we have used if...else when a program needs to choose between two possibilities.

blocks.content: So far, we have used if...else when a program needs to choose between two possibilities.

blocks.text: But what if there are several possible choices?

blocks.content: For example, imagine a program that receives a number from 1 to 5 and displays a corresponding rating:

- 1 → Poor
- 2 → Fair
- 3 → Good
- 4 → Very Good
- 5 → Excellent
Writing many if...else if conditions for this can make the code harder to read.

blocks.text: Java provides the switch statement to handle multiple fixed choices more clearly.

blocks.content: Let's look at its syntax next.

lessons.title: switch Statement
lessons.summary: A switch statement lets us compare one value with several possible options.

blocks.content: A switch statement lets us compare one value with several possible options.

blocks.text: Syntax

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: The value inside switch is compared with each case.

- If it matches option1, that case runs.
- If it matches option2, the second case runs.
- If none of the cases match, default runs.
The break statement stops the switch after the matching case finishes. Without break, Java can continue into the following cases. We'll explore that behavior later.

lessons.title: Removing break from a switch Statement
lessons.summary: The break statement normally stops a switch after the matching case. What happens if we leave it out?

blocks.content: The break statement normally stops a switch after the matching case. What happens if we leave it out?

blocks.text: Let's use a simple example with different menu options.

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: Suppose the user enters 2.

blocks.code:
Edit Profile
Logout
Invalid Choice
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.content: The matching case is case 2, so Edit Profile is printed first.
Because there is no break, Java continues executing the cases below it. Therefore, case 3 and default also run.

blocks.text: This behavior is called fall-through in a switch statement.

lessons.title: Checking for a Leap Year
lessons.summary: A year can be identified as a leap year using a few simple divisibility rules:

blocks.content: A year can be identified as a leap year using a few simple divisibility rules:

- A year divisible by 400 is a leap year.
- A year divisible by 100 but not by 400 is not a leap year.
- A year divisible by 4 and not by 100 is a leap year.
- Any other year is not a leap year.
For example:

- 2024 → Leap year
- 2100 → Not a leap year
- 2400 → Leap year
- 2023 → Not a leap year
Let's implement this logic in Java.
